Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Nobody has to share their own circles or what’s in their backpack. Keep the turn-and-talk open: for you, or for people you know.

Every student in the room

Every student carries something, in every skin tone and every kind of family. Money, being the only one, adult jobs at home and long commutes are often invisible at an independent school; name them plainly and move on so nobody feels spotted.

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Open warm: “Today is about why this toolkit exists. Short version: your life doesn’t come in separate pieces.”

Slide 2 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Ask the room: “Maya gets five hours of sleep. What happens to the rest of her day?” Take two or three guesses, then click on.

Slide 3 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Tired brains run short on patience first. Ask: “Ever been mean to someone who didn’t deserve it, just because you were wiped?”

Slide 4 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Sleep is when the brain files what you learned. Less sleep, messier filing.

Slide 5 · Notes

1 MINUTE. One rough morning starts costing her people. Nobody did anything wrong here.

Slide 6 · Notes

2 MINUTES. Point at the loop: one short night touched home, school, friends and her phone, then made the next night short too. Ask: “Where could the loop break?” Any answer counts.

Slide 7 · Notes

2 MINUTES. Trace one stream with your hand into the lake. Ask: “Which stream has the most water in it for people your age right now?”

Slide 8 · Notes

2 MINUTES. Keep it simple: “You’re never just one thing. A Tuesday feels different depending on all of it at once.” No one has to share their own circles.

Slide 9 · Notes

2 MINUTES. Don’t ask anyone what’s in their backpack. Say: “You can’t tell from the outside, and that’s the point.”

Slide 10 · Notes

4 MINUTES. Turn and talk, then take a few answers. The next four slides show one each; click after the room has had a go.

Slide 11 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Name it plainly. Being “the only one” takes energy most people never notice spending.

Slide 12 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Say it plainly and move on; nobody should feel spotted. Money shapes plans, friendships and stress, and it’s often invisible at a school like ours.

Slide 13 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Lots of students carry adult jobs at home. It can be a source of pride and a real load on the same day.

Slide 14 · Notes

1 MINUTE. When someone seems checked out, sometimes they’re just out of hours.

Slide 15 · Notes

4 MINUTES. Same turn and talk, the other direction. This is the half people forget: identity is a source of strength, too. Three examples follow, one per slide.

Slide 16 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Ask: “Who’s someone in your life who has been through something hard and came out okay?” No need to share out loud.

Slide 17 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Keep it wide on purpose: some students’ steadying thing is a faith, some a grandmother’s cooking, some a team. All count.

Slide 18 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Code-switching is tiring, and it’s also a skill most adults wish they had. Both are true.

Slide 19 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Let the line sit. This is the whole reason the toolkit exists.

Slide 20 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Agency matters here: nobody has to use any of it. Use what helps, skip what doesn’t.

Slide 21 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Name the real people: “Ms. Garcia, Dr. Wilson, your advisor. Our doors are open.”

Slide 22 · Notes

4 MINUTES. Take a few answers; any connection counts.

Slide 23 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Close warm. Point out where to find the toolkit and that every page lists a person first.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students see that sleep, family, school, friends, phones and who they are all run into the same place: how they’re doing. They hear the word intersectionality, notice that every student carries something others can’t see, and that what they carry can also hold them up. They leave knowing the toolkit is there to take what helps, and that a person comes first.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The Student Toolkit link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 5 minMaya’s day: one short night, one slide per link, and the loop
  2. 5 minIt all runs to the same place, and the word for it: intersectionality
  3. 8 minEveryone carries a different backpack: what makes a hard week harder, one answer per slide
  4. 6 minWhat people draw on, one answer per slide
  5. 6 minMental health is where it all meets, take what helps, start with a person, turn and talk, close

Short on time (15 minutes)

Maya’s night and the loop slide, it all runs to the same place, intersectionality, the backpack slide, one harder and one draw-on answer, then mental health is where it all meets and the closing slide.

Before you teach
Nobody speaks for a group.

Invite answers about “you, or people you know.” Never ask a student to explain their culture, faith or family to the room.

Name the load and the strength.

The harder slides and the draw-on slides belong together. Identity can make a week harder and can also be what holds someone up.

Money is real here.

Say it plainly once and keep going. The “I’m good, I already ate” slide works because it doesn’t point at anyone.

If something heavy comes up.

Thank the student, keep it short in the room, and connect them with a counselor that day.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Everyone carries something.

Show the range on purpose: students of every skin tone, family shape and income carry things others can’t see.

Families draw on different things.

Faith, food, music, elders, a team, a language. Treat each as a real strength, never as a curiosity.

Money shapes friendships.

Trips, dinners out and the right shoes cost money. Students with less often do quiet math nobody sees.

Two worlds is a skill.

Students who switch languages or settings all day are tired and skilled at once. Both are true.

What the research says

The term intersectionality comes from legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw, who used it to describe how race and sex together shaped Black women’s experiences in ways neither one alone explains.

Crenshaw, 1989, University of Chicago Legal Forum

Teens aged 13 to 18 need 8 to 10 hours of sleep a night for health, learning, mood and attention.

American Academy of Sleep Medicine consensus statement (Paruthi et al., 2016, Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine)

Across many studies, a positive sense of ethnic-racial identity is linked to better well-being and fewer depressive symptoms in young people.

Rivas-Drake et al., 2014, Child Development

Teens who felt connected at school had lower risks of emotional distress, suicidal thoughts and substance use as adults.

Steiner et al., 2019, JAMA Pediatrics
